name: PSI-10 (ACME Flame Design)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design (ACME/Flame Design)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - ACME modular hardware (spherical porous burner & tri-coflow burner)
fuel_form: Gaseous fuels (ethylene C2H4, methane CH4, hydrogen) with N2 or CO2 inert dilutions (normal and inverse spherical/coflow diffusion flames)
fuel_size: Spherical porous burner
flow_speed: Controlled reactant mass flow rates (normal and inverse convection directions; e.g., 9.2-12.7 mg/s)
objective: Obtain soot-inception limits, radiative/kinetic extinction limits, and detailed flame structure/temperature measurements for quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames (C2H4 and CH4) aboard the ISS.
variables: Flame type (normal vs. inverse), fuel type (C2H4, CH4), oxygen mole fraction (21% to 85%), inert diluent (N2, CO2) placement (Zst), flow rate, pressure (~0.95-1.05 atm)
sensors: Broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), thermocouples, acoustic laser-induced plasma thermometry

insights.habitable_environments: Tested oxygen concentrations up to 85% and CO2/N2 dilution extinction limits, establishing critical radiative and kinetic extinction thresholds (e.g., peak temperature < 1130 K) relevant to high-O2 spacecraft and lunar habitats.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides 121 ISS flight test runs plus drop-tower data defining exact C/O soot-inception limits, pseudo-flammability limits, and radiative/kinetic extinction boundaries for validating combustion models.
insights.earth_benefits: Enables soot-free, high-efficiency oxygen-enhanced combustion strategies and directly contributes to novel designs for cleaner, lower-emission terrestrial combustors and future coal power plants.

relevance_notes: Features 121 ISS runs up to 85% O2 and CO2/N2 extinction limits; supports predictive flammability/extinction modeling and clean terrestrial combustor design.

name: PSI-20 (ACME BRE)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE): Experimental Investigation of Emulated Burning Rate at Various Gravity Levels
period: Approximately 15 years (2010-2025); end date format ambiguous in source
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) / ACME; Burning Rate Emulator porous circular burner
fuel_form: Gaseous fuel (CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures) through a porous burner emulating condensed fuels
fuel_size: Porous circular burners of 25 mm and 50 mm diameter
flow_speed: Quiescent ambient (no forced flow); fuel flow rate through the burner varied
gravity_level: Microgravity (ISS), supported by normal-gravity and drop-facility tests
objective: Establish burning conditions in quiescent microgravity in terms of material properties, by observing quasi-steady burning and extinction limits of gas-fed flames emulating condensed fuels in O2/N2 (and desirably O2/CO2) atmospheres, including those considered for human missions.
variables: Burner diameter (25, 50 mm), fuel mixture (CH4/N2, C2H4/N2), diluent, O2 concentration (21 to 40% in the experimental table), chamber pressure (planned 14.7, 10.2, 8.2 psia), fuel flow rate; observed burner surface temperature, heat flux, flame behavior, ignition and extinction.
sensors: Heat flux sensor (with a temperature limit) and burner surface temperature measurement; flame observation. Further specifications not provided.

insights.habitable_environments: Preliminary flight results show quasi-steady burning without air flow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, while 21% O2 flames self-extinguished quickly. This questions sole reliance on ventilation shutdown for fire suppression in such atmospheres.
insights.predictive_modeling: Aims to map flammability as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation and applied heat flux, heat of combustion, and smoke point, with a CFD model of quiescent microgravity burning intended as a possible predictive method. Quantitative model results are not in the supplied material.
insights.earth_benefits: The emulator is intended to be validated for 1-g use and to establish normal-gravity ignition and extinction limits for gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. No other terrestrial applications are stated.

relevance_notes: Investigators suggest NASA may make more use of the cone calorimeter (Test 2), which measures the material properties matching BRE flames. Results are preliminary. Hardware is CIR/ACME.

name: PSI-21 (ACME CLD Flame)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame): Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) with ACME hardware, International Space Station
fuel_form: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene gaseous jet in coflow laminar diffusion flames
flow_speed: Weak coflow with varied inlet velocity (values not supplied); listed methane tests used fuel and N2 mass flow controllers rated 0.1 slpm max (nitrogen basis)
objective: Produce benchmark data for rigorous testing of computational flame models at the extremes of fuel dilution: (A) flame shape, lift-off height, temperature and extinction limits of weak methane and ethylene coflow diffusion flames versus velocity and dilution; (B) soot tendencies of long-residence-time flames, via flame shape, soot-free gas temperature, soot luminosity, soot temperature and soot volume fraction.
variables: Independent: fuel type (methane, ethylene), nitrogen dilution of fuel (e.g., 25%-40% CH4 by volume in the listed tests), and coflow velocity. Dependent: flame shape, lift-off height, flame temperature, extinction limits, soot luminosity, soot temperature, soot volume fraction.
sensors: OH* and CH* chemiluminescence imaging; soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements; thin-filament pyrometry for non-sooting flame temperature; model-derived species estimates where direct measurement is not possible.

insights.habitable_environments: Extinction-limit and flame-shape data from a real microgravity environment could inform models of fire behavior in spacecraft and future habitats. The supplied material does not discuss spacecraft fire safety explicitly, and no implementation is claimed.
insights.predictive_modeling: The investigation was designed to validate and refine detailed kinetics and soot sub-models, and to use validated simulations to infer species that cannot be measured directly. No quantitative results were supplied.
insights.earth_benefits: Per the source, better prediction of diffusion flames (the type in most practical combustors) can aid modeling of turbulent reacting flows, soot formation and radiative transfer, flame extinction for fire suppression, and engine efficiency.

relevance_notes: Benchmark dataset for diffusion-flame model validation at both ends of the dilution range, with a long publication record (CH* and heat release, soot in normal and microgravity, dilution, velocity, pressure and gravity effects). Shares the coflow burner with PSI-22 (E-FIELD Flames). Source page lists 33 test rows, of which only 5 methane rows were supplied.

name: PSI-22 (E-FIELD Flames)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the ISS with gas-jet and coflow burners and a high-voltage copper mesh electrode
fuel_form: Gaseous laminar diffusion flames (methane and ethylene, nitrogen-diluted), with and without air coflow
flow_speed: Fuel flow rate and coflow velocity varied (weak synthetic air coflow); values not provided
objective: Understand how electric field voltage relates to chemi-ion current, how flames respond dynamically to field changes, how soot formation is affected, and how stabilized near-limit lifted flames behave.
variables: Independent: field strength (up to 10 kV), mesh polarity, fuel (CH4, C2H4), nitrogen dilution, fuel flow rate, coflow velocity. Dependent: ion current, flame response time, flame shape and luminosity, soot distribution and volume fraction, chemiluminescence, radiant emission.
sensors: Voltage-current curves, high-resolution cameras, filtered spectral imaging for chemiluminescence and soot volume fraction, thermopile detectors for radiant emission.

insights.habitable_environments: Not conducted for space applications per the investigators; findings may possibly inform future space-based combustion devices such as solid waste processing. No direct spacecraft fire detection or suppression application is claimed.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides buoyancy-free data on ion-driven convection, ion current and flame response to electric fields, useful as reference behavior for flame and chemi-ionization models. Results were not included in the supplied material.
insights.earth_benefits: Electric-field control of flames could reduce pollutant and soot emissions and possibly improve combustion efficiency and fuel use, as stated by the investigators; these are potential benefits, not demonstrated outcomes.

relevance_notes: Fundamental ISS study of laminar diffusion flames as electrically active systems, sharing the coflow burner with the CLD Flame experiment (PSI-21) and linked to PSI-23. Design and objectives are documented; results, oxygen concentration, pressure and flow values were not supplied.

name: PSI-23 (ACME s-Flame)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) with ACME hardware on the International Space Station; spherical porous burner
fuel_form: Gaseous fuel/diluent mixtures (H2/CH4/diluent for soot-free flames; C2H4/diluent for sooty flames) issued from a spherical porous burner
flow_speed: Varied reactant flow rates through the spherical porous burner (specific values not provided)
objective: Characterize the transient structure of nominally spherical, one-dimensional diffusion flames (soot-free and sooty), determine their convective/chemical-kinetic and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits, and establish whether, when and how pulsating instabilities predicted by theory occur, using the data to test detailed chemical kinetic and transport models.
variables: Fuel type (hydrogen, methane, ethylene); fuel/diluent ratio; diluent type (nitrogen and helium to adjust diffusivity, carbon dioxide to alter radiation); reactant flow rate; ambient temperature and pressure; system Damkohler number; Zeldovich number; Lewis number of the fuel/diluent mixture.
sensors: Spectrally resolved flame imaging (including chemiluminescence), flame and burner temperature measurements, radiative flux measurements, and logging of operating conditions (reactant flow rates, ambient temperature, pressure, acceleration levels). Measurements are synchronized and compared with detailed numerical simulations.

insights.habitable_environments: The investigation maps where gaseous diffusion flames stop burning (extinction limits driven by convection/kinetics at low Damkohler number and by radiation/kinetics at high Damkohler number) in a buoyancy-free setting aboard the ISS. This is baseline knowledge on how flames persist or die out in microgravity; direct application to spacecraft fire safety is a potential implication and is not stated in the supplied material.
insights.predictive_modeling: Each flame measurement (structure, front velocity, steady-state and extinction conditions, instabilities, soot suppression limits) serves as a stringent test of a transient simulation that includes detailed chemistry, transport and radiation models. The simulation is also used to define the flight test matrix, so experiment and model are developed together.
insights.earth_benefits: Diffusion-flame burning underlies many combustion engines and devices, so a better grasp of its dynamics and chemistry can help improve power, efficiency, pollutant emissions and reliability. The buoyancy-free environment also yields simple flow fields for high-fidelity data on unit thermochemical processes and their physico-chemical parameters.

relevance_notes: Fundamental, model-validation-oriented flame study on the ISS CIR. The supplied material lists objectives, approach and a long publication record but no flight results. Related to PSI-22; no formal dependency on other investigations is stated.

name: PSI-25 (BASS-II)
full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with small wind tunnel on the ISS
fuel_form: Rods, spherical sections, slabs, films and fabric sheets
fuel_size: Includes PMMA films 2 cm wide, 100-300 micron thick; other sizes not stated
flow_speed: Forced flow up to 40 cm/s, opposed and concurrent
objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity, test whether NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 is conservative for space, and provide preliminary data for SoFIE investigators.
variables: Forced flow speed and direction (opposed vs concurrent), ambient O2 concentration (reduced below 21% by nitrogen dilution), and sample geometry and thickness. Recorded: initial/final O2 and CO2 (% by volume), initial/final CO (ppm), radiometer gain, frames shot.
sensors: MSG imaging (flame appearance, growth and spread rates), radiometer, O2, CO2 and CO measurements, on-board CSA-CP and CDM sensors.

insights.habitable_environments: Tests whether Earth-based upward-burning flammability screening is conservative for spacecraft, supporting safer material selection and firefighting approaches for future crewed vehicles and habitats. Implementation in standards is not stated.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides spherical-like, buoyancy-free flame data for validating computational combustion models used to design detection and suppression systems; publications cover flame-spread regimes, extinction limits and narrow-channel analogues.
insights.earth_benefits: Validated models can inform analysis of wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling and other combustion problems.

relevance_notes: Related to PSI-26; supplies preliminary data to SoFIE PIs. Supplied material lacks quantitative results; pressure and minimum O2 are not stated.

name: PSI-26 (BASS)
full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) - 76 mm x 76 mm modular fan-driven flow duct (SPICE flow duct)
fuel_form: Custom Sibal fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), Nomex fabric, Ultem, PMMA spheres and cylinders
fuel_size: 1-2 cm samples (e.g., 2 cm Sibal, 1-2 cm PMMA spheres) inside a 76 mm x 76 mm cross-section duct
flow_speed: Up to 40 cm/s variable-speed forced airflow (concurrent and opposed flow)
objective: Bridge the gap between normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 and actual microgravity material flammability over extended ISS burn times, and assess inert gaseous extinguishing agent (nitrogen) effectiveness across materials, geometries, preheating, and airflow.
variables: Airflow velocity (up to 40 cm/s), flow direction (concurrent vs. opposed), sample material (Sibal, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA), geometry (flat fabrics, spheres, cylinders, wake flames), thickness, preheating, inert suppressant (nitrogen)
sensors: Top and edge profile video cameras, radiometers, thermocouples

insights.habitable_environments: Proves that with adequate ventilation (up to 40 cm/s), solid spacecraft materials (fabrics, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA) can burn as well as or even better in microgravity than in 1g, revealing critical gaps in standard 1g NASA-STD-6001 material screening.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 123 ISS microgravity test runs measuring flame spread rates, radiative heat emission, and quenching limits across concurrent and opposed flows to validate solid combustion and heat-release models.
insights.earth_benefits: Validates simplified low-gravity combustion physics that serve as foundational building blocks for complex normal-gravity fire models and performance-based fire safety standards on Earth.

relevance_notes: Foundational ISS solid-fuel flammability and nitrogen-suppression study (123 runs) inside MSG; directly informs spacecraft material selection (NASA-STD-6001) and habitable cabin ventilation limits. Related to PSI-25 (BASS-II follow-on) and PSI-107 (SPICE, whose flow duct it reuses).

name: PSI-39 (CFI)
full_name: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
fuel_form: Liquid hydrocarbon fuel droplets (n-dodecane C12H26, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, farnesane) suspended or tethered on SiC fibers
fuel_size: Single suspended or fiber-tethered liquid fuel droplets
flow_speed: Quiescent chamber atmosphere (controlled gas mixture delivery)
objective: Examine low-temperature cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and farnesane droplets across pressures (0.25-5 atm) and helium dilutions aboard the ISS, linking droplet size, pressure, soot formation, and flame extinction.
variables: Fuel composition (n-dodecane, iso-dodecane mixtures, farnesane), chamber pressure (0.25 to 5 atm), diluent gases (O2, N2, Helium), droplet diameter, tethering method (free-floating vs. SiC fiber)
sensors: Black-and-white camera (droplet sizing), UV camera (OH* radical emissions and flame size), high-resolution cameras, narrow-band and wide-band radiometers

insights.habitable_environments: Reveals how helium dilution, reduced cabin pressures (down to 0.25 atm / ~3.7 psi), and droplet size govern low-temperature cool-flame extinction in microgravity, supporting safer spacecraft fire-suppression and pressure envelopes.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 88 ISS microgravity test runs measuring droplet extinction diameters, OH* radical emissions, and radiative heat flux across pressures (0.25-5 atm) to validate low-temperature chemical kinetic models.
insights.earth_benefits: Advances fuel ignition and low-temperature kinetic modeling needed to design clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines and predict octane/cetane ratings for spark-ignition and diesel fuels.

relevance_notes: Core ISS droplet cool-flame study (88 runs) in CIR/MDCA across sub-atmospheric to elevated pressures (0.25-5 atm) and helium dilution; related to PSI-69.

name: PSI-47 (DAFT / DAFT-2)
full_name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 (DAFT / DAFT-2)
hardware: ISS Express Rack 4 / Port Rack 6 / Node 1 - Modified TSI P-Trak (capillary alcohol wick) & DustTrak CNC
fuel_form: Aerosolized Arizona Road Dust (ARD Fine) dispersed with GN2 in 15-liter Mylar bags and ambient cabin particulates
fuel_size: Fine dust/aerosol particulates (sub-micron to micron scale)
flow_speed: Internal instrument sampling airflow
objective: Demonstrate the functionality and accuracy of a microgravity-modified TSI P-Trak condensate nuclei counter (using capillary forces for isopropyl alcohol recycling) compared against a DustTrak control aboard the ISS to de-risk the SAME investigation.
variables: Instrument type (modified TSI P-Trak vs. DustTrak), aerosol source (Arizona Road Dust in 15L Mylar bags vs. ISS cabin/Velcro particulates), sampling location (Express Rack 4, Port Rack 6, Node 1)
sensors: Modified TSI P-Trak condensate nuclei counter (laser particle counter with capillary alcohol wick), DustTrak optical aerosol monitor

insights.habitable_environments: Validates reliable microgravity aerosol and dust counting instruments capable of distinguishing nuisance dust (such as lunar regolith dust or Velcro debris) from combustion smoke inside spacecraft and lunar habitats.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides 3 ISS on-orbit calibration and validation sessions comparing modified capillary-wick condensation particle counters against DustTrak benchmarks in zero gravity.
insights.earth_benefits: Informs the design of orientation-independent, high-sensitivity particulate and smoke detectors for extreme confined Earth environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories.

relevance_notes: De-risked and validated the particle counting instrumentation for SAME (PSI-102); critical for differentiating nuisance dust from fire smoke in spacecraft and lunar bases.

name: PSI-60 (SPICE Soot Analysis)
full_name: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
hardware: Computational Soot/Flow-Species Model & Color-Ratio Pyrometry (Validated against ISS SPICE MSG and Yale/ACME burner data)
fuel_form: Gaseous co-flow laminar diffusion flames
fuel_size: Yale and ACME burner configurations
flow_speed: Co-flow laminar airflow (microgravity vs. normal gravity)
gravity_level: Ground Investigation (Reconciling Microgravity SPICE & Normal-Gravity Data)
objective: Integrate computational soot modeling and color-ratio pyrometry on over 1,600 raw DSLR images from the ISS Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions, reconciling discrepancies between 0g and 1g soot formation.
variables: Gravity regime (microgravity vs. normal gravity), burner configuration (Yale vs. ACME), radiation re-absorption, scattering, heat transfer to burner structure
sensors: Nikon DSLR cameras (1,600+ raw NEF images analyzed via 3-channel color-ratio pyrometry and absolute light calibration)

insights.habitable_environments: Demonstrates that microgravity flames are longer, cooler, and produce significantly higher soot concentrations than 1g flames, directly informing smoke generation and fire detection thresholds inside crewed spacecraft.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers a coupled flow-species-soot computational framework incorporating radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate growth to reconcile 0g and 1g smoke-point predictions.
insights.earth_benefits: Improves soot formation and radiative transport models to reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and design cleaner industrial and energy systems on Earth.

relevance_notes: Depends on ISS SPICE data (PSI-107). Reconciles 0g vs. 1g soot formation across 1,600+ DSLR images to improve spacecraft fire detection and soot modeling.

name: PSI-62 (FGM Flame Spread Modeling)
full_name: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
hardware: Unsteady Flamelet Generated Manifold (UFGM) CFD Framework (Validated against ISS BASS / BASS-II MSG flight data)
fuel_form: Solid fuels subject to charring and ablation (PMMA flat sheets, spheres, rods, and wax cylinders)
fuel_size: Various BASS geometries (flat sheets, spheres, rods, cylinders)
flow_speed: Concurrent forced airflow (reproducing the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone)
objective: Develop and validate unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) CFD modeling techniques for concurrent solid-fuel flame spread in microgravity using NASA BASS and BASS-II data to accurately predict flammability limits for spacecraft materials.
variables: Fuel material and geometry (PMMA flat sheets, spheres, rods; wax cylinders), charring/ablation response, concurrent airflow velocity, gravity regime (microgravity vs. normal gravity)
sensors: Two-color tomography with DSLR cameras (post-processed BASS/BASS-II imagery for 3D soot and temperature reconstruction), two-color pyrometry

insights.habitable_environments: Accurately reproduces the microgravity 'Goldilocks' flammability zone for solid spacecraft materials (such as PMMA), providing a validated screening tool for selecting safer cabin and habitat materials.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers a validated Unsteady Flamelet Generated Manifold (UFGM) subgrid-scale model for Large Eddy Simulations (LES) capable of predicting solid flame geometry, soot volume fraction, temperature fields, and spread rates.
insights.earth_benefits: Improves terrestrial fire safety standards and combustion modeling by deepening understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes in charring and ablating solid fires.

relevance_notes: Depends on BASS (PSI-26) and BASS-II (PSI-25). Directly supports predictive flammability modeling (LES subgrid models) and screening of solid spacecraft materials.

name: PSI-68 (FLEX-2)
full_name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment-2 (FLEX-2): The Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) with Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) on the International Space Station
fuel_form: Liquid fuel droplets (single droplets and binary linear arrays; fiber-supported or freely deployed; pure and bi-component fuels)
fuel_size: Initial droplet diameter 1.5-5 mm (visible experimental table entries)
flow_speed: Droplet translation-generated flow, 0.1-5 cm/s (visible experimental table entries)
objective: Extend FLEX-1 to fuels and conditions resembling real combustors and produce benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion, covering liquid-phase mixing, flame extinction mechanisms and boundaries, soot formation, and droplet-array interactions, to validate numerical simulations and support new theoretical models.
variables: Independent: fuel type, ambient gas composition (O2 with N2 or He diluent), ambient pressure (0.5-3.0 atm), initial droplet diameter, droplet translation velocity and acceleration, droplet spacing and size in binary linear arrays. Oxygen mole fraction 0.1-0.4 in the approach text. Ignitor on-time 1-5 s. Ambient temperature 25 C in visible table entries.
sensors: Color camera with near-real-time video downlink; high-speed photography for flame evolution; chamber pressure and temperature recorded in near real time. No further specifications supplied.

insights.habitable_environments: Aims to provide data on extinction and flammability limits of liquid-fuel flames across oxygen and pressure ranges in real microgravity, which could inform fire-safety analysis for spacecraft and habitats. No resulting design or procedure change is documented in the supplied material.
insights.predictive_modeling: Intended as benchmark data to test simulation assumptions (chemistry, radiation, gas-liquid coupling) and to develop new droplet-combustion theory. No model comparison results were supplied.
insights.earth_benefits: Stated potential benefits include more efficient, cleaner liquid-fuel combustion, low-emission combustor design, fuel surrogate development, and jet engine model validation. These are expected benefits, not demonstrated outcomes.

relevance_notes: Flight droplet-combustion study on the ISS extending FLEX-1 (PSI-69), focused on flame extinction, soot, and bi-component fuels. The supplied material contains no results; about 50 associated publications are listed by title only. Four of nine experimental table entries were not visible.

name: PSI-69 (FLEX)
full_name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
fuel_form: Free-floating and fiber-supported liquid fuel droplets (methanol, n-heptane, n-octane, n-decane, n-butanol, methyl decanoate, Jet-A and biofuels)
fuel_size: ~1.6 to 3 mm initial droplet diameter
flow_speed: Quiescent atmosphere and slow sub-buoyant convective droplet drift
objective: Map microgravity flammability limits (Limiting Oxygen Index) of liquid fuel droplets across pressures (0.5-1.5 atm), measure the suppression effectiveness of gaseous diluents (CO2, He, SF6), and obtain high-resolution burning rate, soot, radiation, and cool-flame extinction data.
variables: Suppressant diluent gas (CO2, He, SF6), ambient pressure (0.5 to 1.5 atm / ~7.35 to 22.05 psi), ambient oxygen mole fraction, initial droplet diameter (~1.6-3 mm), fuel type, droplet drift velocity
sensors: High-speed UV and color cameras, narrow-band and wide-band radiometers, pressure transducers, fiber-optic spectroscopy

insights.habitable_environments: Quantifies the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) and minimum concentrations of inert fire suppressants (CO2, Helium, SF6) required to extinguish fires across sub-atmospheric to elevated cabin pressures (0.5-1.5 atm) in microgravity.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 275 ISS microgravity droplet combustion test runs with exact pressures, initial/extinction droplet diameters, burning rates, and burn times, plus the landmark discovery of two-stage cool-flame droplet burning.
insights.earth_benefits: Informs cleaner, less toxic fire-suppression agents for confined environments (submarines, high-altitude aircraft) and advances low-temperature cool-flame kinetics to improve automotive and industrial engine efficiency.

relevance_notes: Cornerstone ISS fire-suppression investigation (275 test runs) in CIR/MDCA; serves as the foundational flight dataset referenced by follow-on cool-flame studies (PSI-39, PSI-68, PSI-117, PSI-142).

name: PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I)
full_name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
hardware: Saffire-I Enclosure in Cygnus Resupply Vehicle (fan-driven flow duct)
fuel_form: Large-scale Sibal composite fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight)
fuel_size: 0.94 m long x 0.40 m wide x 0.37 cm thick
flow_speed: 20 cm/s forced airflow (concurrent and opposed flow directions)
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and investigate low-g material flammability limits compared to NASA's normal-gravity screening tests inside an uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft.
variables: Airflow direction (concurrent vs. opposed), forced airflow velocity (20 cm/s), ignition power and duration (182 W for 8 s), large sample geometry
sensors: Two video cameras, thermocouples (flow, flame, and plume temperatures), two radiometers, solid-state pressure, CO2, and O2 sensors, two anemometers

insights.habitable_environments: Provides the first realistic large-scale spacecraft fire benchmark (0.94 m x 0.4 m Sibal fabric) in an uncrewed Cygnus module, proving that 1g flammability tests carry significant risk for long-duration crewed habitats and showing concurrent flow burns 6x longer (420 s) than opposed flow (70 s).
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers full-scale microgravity flame spread, burn duration, radiative heat flux, and O2/CO2 consumption data at 20 cm/s airflow to validate transient flame-growth models.
insights.earth_benefits: Directly benefits fire safety, smoke characterization, and prevention efforts inside sealed, confined terrestrial environments such as mines, airplanes, and submarines.

relevance_notes: Foundational large-scale spacecraft fire safety demonstration (Saffire-I) in Cygnus; directly informs habitable cabin material selection and ventilation limits. Related to PSI-99, PSI-100 (follow-on SAFFIRE flights) and PSI-26 (BASS).

name: PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II)
full_name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II)
hardware: SAFFIRE flight unit in the Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module (flow duct with sample card, fans, flow straighteners)
fuel_form: Flat solid samples on a sample card (silicone, cotton-fiberglass SIBAL, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, PMMA with Nomex)
fuel_size: 9 samples per card, each 5 cm x 29 cm; silicone samples in the visible table rows are 0.27 to 1.03 mm thick
flow_speed: 20 or 30 cm/s depending on sample material; concurrent or opposed flow
gravity_level: Microgravity (orbital flight on Cygnus after departure from the ISS)
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with those from NASA's normal-gravity material flammability screening test.
variables: Sample material and thickness, air flow velocity (20 or 30 cm/s), flow direction (concurrent or opposed), ignition power (80 W) and ignition time (9.2 s in the visible rows), and oxygen level (about 21.5 to 22.1 percent in the visible rows; table Note 1 not supplied). Dependent measures include burn time, burn length, flame spread length or rate, flame size, temperatures, flame radiation, pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction, and flow velocity.
sensors: Two cameras for flame imaging; thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperature; two radiometers for flame radiation; solid-state sensors for pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction; two anemometers for flow velocity. Data were compressed and downlinked.

insights.habitable_environments: Provides large-scale fire data in an uncrewed, expendable spacecraft, addressing the lack of microgravity data available to spacecraft designers. Intended to help test whether terrestrial fire standards adequately support fire safety design for exploration vehicles with longer transit times. Applicability to specific habitats is a stated motivation, not a demonstrated result in the supplied material.
insights.predictive_modeling: Supplies microgravity flammability-limit data for several spacecraft materials and supports validation of NASA's material selection criteria. A listed publication compares a transient flame growth model with experiment for a large fabric, indicating the data are used for model evaluation; the model results themselves were not supplied.
insights.earth_benefits: Per the source, studying fire in small sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo vehicle may benefit fire safety and prevention in mines, airplanes and submarines.

relevance_notes: Follow-on to Saffire-I (PSI-98), adding more samples (SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, PMMA with Nomex). Visible table rows show no significant microgravity burning for four silicone samples and full-length burning of a SIBAL sample (145 s burn time), but only 5 of 16 rows were supplied. Related publications cover silicone buoyancy effects, flame spread over PMMA, and fire emission sensors.

name: PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III)
full_name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III (SAFFIRE-III) Investigation
hardware: Saffire III enclosure in Cygnus
fuel_form: SIBAL sample material (specific form not stated in supplied material)
flow_speed: 30 cm/s, concurrent or opposed flow
gravity_level: Microgravity (Cygnus resupply vehicle after deberthing from the ISS)
objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and investigate low-gravity flammability limits compared with those from NASA's normal-gravity material flammability screening test.
variables: Flow direction (concurrent or opposed) at 30 cm/s, versus 20 cm/s in SAFFIRE-I; sample and experimental parameters (detailed in an Experimental Details file not supplied). Measured: flame growth, temperatures, flame radiation, pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction, flow velocity.
sensors: Two cameras for flame imaging; thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperatures; two radiometers for flame radiation; solid-state sensors for pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction; two anemometers for flow velocity. Data compressed and downlinked.

insights.habitable_environments: Intended to give spacecraft designers large-scale microgravity fire data to reduce reliance on terrestrial fire standards, a risk the source says grows on longer exploration missions. Results were not supplied, so no demonstrated design impact is claimed.
insights.predictive_modeling: The combined imaging, temperature, radiation, gas composition and flow data could support validation of NASA's material selection criteria and of models of flame size under limited oxygen. No modeling table or results were supplied.
insights.earth_benefits: The source states that studying fire in small, sealed environments benefits fire safety and prevention on Earth, including in mines, airplanes, and submarines.

relevance_notes: Flight experiment following SAFFIRE-I (PSI-98) with the same SIBAL material at higher flow velocity; related to PSI-99. Performed in an uncrewed vehicle to allow large-scale burning without crew risk. Supplied record contains objectives, approach and hypothesis but no results; the impacts text has minor inconsistencies (references to Saffire-I).

name: PSI-101 (SAME-R)
full_name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (SAME-R)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) - Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware (M-pass instrument, DustTrak, ionization detector, thermal precipitators)
fuel_form: Overheated/pyrolyzing spacecraft materials (Kapton, Pyrell intumescent fire-retardant foam)
fuel_size: Small heated/pyrolyzing samples
flow_speed: 8.1 cm/s inlet velocity (with no-flow during sample heating)
objective: Quantify liquid smoke particulate sizes and droplet size distributions in low gravity aboard the ISS using improved materials (Pyrell foam, Kapton) and diagnostics (M-pass) to relate smoke generation/transport to spacecraft detector response.
variables: Sample material (Pyrell foam, Kapton), heating temperature, flow condition (no-flow heating vs. 8.1 cm/s inlet velocity), primary aging and mixing times
sensors: M-pass instrument (GRC in-house), DustTrak, ionization smoke detector, thermal precipitators (TEM grids)

insights.habitable_environments: Proves that in microgravity, reduced mixing and longer residence times cause smoldering smoke particles to coagulate into substantially larger droplets (with lower number density), which can prevent conventional spacecraft smoke detectors from triggering an alarm.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides 110 documented ISS experimental runs (66 flight test points) with exact inlet velocities (8.1 cm/s), aging times, and validated lognormal moment-method particle distributions to model aerosol growth and detector sensitivity.
insights.earth_benefits: Directly supports the development of advanced, false-alarm-resistant smoke detectors for extreme confined environments on Earth, such as submarines and underwater laboratories.

relevance_notes: Reflight building directly on the original SAME investigation (PSI-102). Essential baseline dataset (110 test runs) for next-generation spacecraft and terrestrial smoke detection.

name: PSI-102 (SAME)
full_name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) - Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware (near-field & far-field boxes, two smoke detectors, thermophoretic soot samplers)
fuel_form: Overheated/pyrolyzing spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, wire insulation)
fuel_size: Small heated/pyrolyzing samples
flow_speed: 5 to 10 cm/s airflow
objective: Quantify liquid smoke particulate sizes and droplet size distributions in low gravity aboard the ISS, relate them to fuel pyrolysis rates and flow environments, and develop a numerical model for smoke droplet growth.
variables: Sample material (Teflon, Kapton), airflow velocity (5 vs. 10 cm/s), weight loss rate (1-2 mg/min), igniter duration (15-60 s), particle aging duration (1-20 min)
sensors: Two spacecraft smoke detectors, video cameras, thermophoretic soot samplers analyzed post-flight via Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)

insights.habitable_environments: Demonstrates that in microgravity, absent buoyancy-driven mixing increases vapor residence time and coagulation, creating larger smoke droplets with lower number density that may fail to trigger conventional spacecraft smoke detectors.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides 9 controlled ISS test runs (Teflon and Kapton at 5-10 cm/s airflow, 1-20 min aging) plus 1g mass-loss-matched benchmarks to validate numerical smoke droplet growth models.
insights.earth_benefits: Establishes the foundational reduced-gravity smoke baseline used to engineer reliable, life-saving smoke detectors for extreme confined terrestrial habitats such as submarines and underwater laboratories.

relevance_notes: Foundational ISS smoke characterization study (SAME) inside MSG; establishes the baseline dataset for spacecraft and terrestrial smoke detectors (followed by SAME-R / PSI-101). Also related to PSI-47 (DAFT, instrument de-risking) and PSI-115 (modeling).

name: PSI-106 (SLICE)
full_name: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) - modular fan-driven flow duct (built for SPICE) with exchangeable burner tubes
fuel_form: Gaseous laminar co-flow diffusion flames (methane CH4, ethylene C2H4, and N2-diluted mixtures: 100% CH4, 70% CH4, 40% CH4, 20% C2H4)
fuel_size: Exchangeable burner tubes (varying burner diameters)
flow_speed: Controlled co-flow air velocity (testing flame liftoff velocity limits)
objective: Investigate the structure, base stabilization mechanisms, liftoff velocity limits, soot formation, and radiative heat loss of laminar co-flow diffusion flames in microgravity across different fuels, N2 dilutions, and burner diameters.
variables: Fuel type (CH4, C2H4), nitrogen fuel dilution (100%, 70%, 40% CH4; 20% C2H4), burner tube diameter, co-flow air velocity
sensors: High-resolution still camera (4,000+ images with overlaid sensor data), flow rate sensors, temperature sensors, pyrometry diagnostics

insights.habitable_environments: Quantifies flame base stabilization and liftoff velocity limits under forced ventilation co-flows in microgravity, helping define safe spacecraft airflow speeds to prevent flame anchoring or blow-off hazards.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 13 ISS test runs and over 4,000 high-resolution sensor-overlaid images correlating burner diameter, N2 dilution, and co-flow velocity with flame length, soot, and radiative heat loss to validate 0g vs. 1g numerical models.
insights.earth_benefits: Improves numerical models of flame stability and soot inception, directly informing the design of cleaner, lower-emission terrestrial engines and industrial burners.

relevance_notes: Conducted in MSG using the modular fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE (PSI-107). Provides 13 ISS runs and 4,000+ images on co-flow flame liftoff limits and soot formation for predictive modeling.

name: PSI-107 (SPICE)
full_name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ISS
fuel_form: Gas-jet laminar diffusion flames in co-flowing air
fuel_size: Burner nozzle diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm
flow_speed: Co-flow air velocity from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s
objective: Identify laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under varied co-flow conditions in microgravity; determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on luminous flame length and smoke point; quantify sooting propensity of fuels (ethylene, propane, propylene mixtures); and validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time.
variables: Independent: fuel type (methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, propylene mixtures), burner diameter, co-flow air velocity, fuel flow rate. Dependent: smoke point (flame transition to soot emission), luminous flame length/height, radiative heat loss, co-flow velocity distribution. 526 flames studied.
sensors: Still and video cameras for flame length and shape; measurements of radiative heat loss and co-flow air velocity distributions. Specific instrument models and specifications not provided.

insights.habitable_environments: Intended to improve understanding of soot formation and support design of safer spacecraft environments. Applicability to future habitats is a potential implication; no results or implementation are reported in the supplied material.
insights.predictive_modeling: Data on non-buoyant flame lengths, shapes and smoke points are intended to refine computational models of flame behavior without buoyancy and to test the flame shape and residence time correlation. Quantitative outcomes were not supplied.
insights.earth_benefits: Stated potential benefits include better understanding of soot generation and possible insights into fuel formulations and combustion processes.

relevance_notes: Fire-safety-focused microgravity combustion study of soot onset in co-flow jet flames, run in the MSG on the ISS. Its data and hardware are used by PSI-60 (SPICE data analysis), PSI-106 (SLICE) and PSI-26 (BASS flow duct). Results are not included in the supplied material; table counts (470 entries) differ from the 526 flames stated.

name: PSI-115 (SAME Smoke Modeling)
full_name: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
hardware: Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) Navier-Stokes Nodal Model (Validated against ISS SAME MSG data)
fuel_form: Pyrolysis vapor / dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) liquid smoke aerosol particles
fuel_size: Sub-micron to micron aerosol particles in heated sample wake
flow_speed: Two low-speed cross-flow velocities (buoyant vs. non-buoyant wake regimes)
objective: Use direct numerical simulation (DNS) validated against ISS Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) data to quantify differences between microgravity and 1g pyrolysis smoke growth and identify the governing fluid dynamic mechanisms.
variables: Gravity level (0g vs. 1g), cross-flow velocity (two low-speed regimes), thermophoresis, particle settling, wake flow geometry, material composition
sensors: Simulated scalar fields and particle size distributions reconciled with ISS SAME aerosol diagnostics

insights.habitable_environments: Demonstrates that without buoyancy, reduced mixing and altered time-temperature histories trap smoke precursors in the wake, significantly changing particle trajectories and size distributions inside spacecraft cabins.
insights.predictive_modeling: Provides a high-fidelity Navier-Stokes DNS modeling framework validated against SAME flight data that quantifies how gravity, thermophoresis, and cross-flow velocities govern smoke aerosol growth.
insights.earth_benefits: Delivers predictive smoke-characterization models that improve terrestrial fire-detection sensor design and help prevent fires causing loss of life and materiel.

relevance_notes: Depends on ISS SAME data (PSI-102). Explains the fluid-dynamic mechanisms behind 0g vs. 1g smoke aerosol differences to advance spacecraft and terrestrial fire detection.

name: PSI-117 (Cool Flame CFD)
full_name: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
hardware: OpenFOAM 3D CFD Model (Validated against ISS FLEX / MDCA flight data)
fuel_form: Liquid fuel droplets (n-alkane, n-heptane/iso-octane, jet fuel surrogates)
fuel_size: Large (1-4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets
flow_speed: Controlled convective drift and oscillatory shear inflow
objective: Quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulate droplet cool flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction in microgravity using 3D CFD validated against ISS FLEX data.
variables: Perturbation forcing mode (convection, heat flux, combined), amplitude, frequency, droplet diameter (0.5-4 mm), ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), pressure
sensors: CFD Observables (ignition delay, oscillation frequency/amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters) reconciled with FLEX measurements

insights.habitable_environments: In microgravity, minor convective drift from cabin ventilation or external heat flux can drive invisible liquid-droplet cool flames to oscillate or transition back into hot flames instead of extinguishing, requiring spacecraft fire detection and ventilation limits to account for cool-flame re-ignition risks.
insights.predictive_modeling: Reconciles 3D OpenFOAM multi-physics CFD simulations with ISS FLEX flight data to deliver validated stability maps, ignition delays, and extinction diameters across droplet sizes (0.5-4 mm) and flow perturbations.
insights.earth_benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion chemistry and validated CFD tools directly transferable to terrestrial internal combustion engines to mitigate engine knock, improve fuel efficiency, and reduce emissions.

relevance_notes: Depends on ISS FLEX flight data (PSI-69) and is related to PSI-142. Supports predictive flammability modeling (stability maps) and improves spacecraft fire-safety envelopes by resolving cool-flame re-ignition and extinction limits.

name: PSI-142 (Counterflow Cool Flames)
full_name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
hardware: Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware (Counterflow burner & 1D numerical modeling schemes)
fuel_form: Counterflow diffusion flames and 1D freely-propagating mixtures (n-heptane, dimethyl ether DME, large n-alkanes, methane)
fuel_size: One-dimensional counterflow geometry
flow_speed: Controlled counterflow stretch / convective strain rate
gravity_level: Ground Investigation (Extending ISS FLEX Microgravity Data)
objective: Use ISS Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) data to conduct ground-based ozone-sensitized counterflow experiments and simulations that map cool-flame flammability and extinction limits under radiation, diffusion, and convection, bridging hot and cool flame limits.
variables: Oxygen concentration, ozone (O3) sensitization, diluent concentration, pressure (up to 20 atm / ~294 psi), counterflow stretch rate, fuel type (n-heptane, DME, large n-alkanes, CH4)
sensors: CH2O Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF), thermometry, intermediate species (HO2/H2O2) diagnostics

insights.habitable_environments: Bridges the gap between hot-flame and cool-flame extinction limits across oxygen, dilution, and flow-stretch conditions, helping prevent unexpected cool-to-warm-to-hot flame transitions in spacecraft cabins.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 9 quantitative experimental/modeling datasets (CFE/HFE extinction limits, CH2O PLIF, and thermometry) plus cool-flame flammability diagrams to validate kinetic and radiation models.
insights.earth_benefits: Identifies the double reaction zone of warm flames and proves that elevated pressures (20-40 atm) expand cool/warm flame regimes, directly informing high-pressure engine efficiency and emissions control.

relevance_notes: Depends on ISS FLEX data (PSI-69). Provides quantitative cool/warm/hot flame extinction diagrams and 9 datasets for validating predictive kinetic and radiation models.

name: PSI-159 (ACME CFI-G)
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (ACME CFI-G)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - ACME modular hardware (spherical porous burner)
fuel_form: Gaseous fuels (ethane, propane, n-butane, n-pentane) with reactant dilutions on spherical porous burners (normal and inverse flames)
fuel_size: Spherical porous burner
flow_speed: Controlled reactant flow rates (normal and inverse convection directions; e.g., 10.5-12 mg/s fuel flow)
objective: Determine the conditions for steady-state spherical cool diffusion flames (normal and inverse) for ethane, propane, n-butane, and n-pentane aboard the ISS, and validate chemical kinetics mechanisms and CFD simulations.
variables: Fuel type (ethane, propane, n-butane, n-pentane), flame type (normal vs. inverse), oxygen concentration (up to 85%), reactant dilution, flow rate, pressure, stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst), adiabatic flame temperature (Tad)
sensors: Broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), thermocouples

insights.habitable_environments: Conducted the highest oxygen concentration microgravity tests in PSI (up to 85% O2), directly bounding extreme flammability risks for 30%+ O2 lunar bases, pressurized rovers, and 100% O2 spacesuits.
insights.predictive_modeling: Delivers 180 documented ISS test runs (normal and inverse spherical flames) with exact O2 levels, pressures (~0.94 bar / 13.7 psi), flow rates, and cool-flame temperatures (500-1000 K) to validate chemical kinetics and CFD models.
insights.earth_benefits: Advances cool-flame chemical kinetics mechanisms (500-1000 K) needed to enable ultra-lean internal combustion engines, potentially raising thermal efficiency from <=38% up to 60% while reducing emissions.

relevance_notes: Highest O2 tests in PSI (up to 85% O2); critical benchmark for high-O2 habitable spacecraft/lunar environments and predictive cool-flame modeling.
